text: Ghulam Ishaq Khan (20 January 1915 – 27 October 2006), commonly known as GIK, was a Pakistani bureaucrat, politician, and statesman who served as the seventh president of Pakistan from 1988 to 1993. Prior to this, he held the position of chairman of the Senate from 1985 to 1988 under President Zia-ul-Haq and assumed the presidency following Zia's death in an air crash on 17 August 1988. Born in Ismail Khel, a rural area near Bannu in the North-West Frontier Province (now Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa), Khan was a Pashtun of the Bangash tribe. He graduated from Peshawar University with double BSc degrees in Chemistry and Botany, attending Islamia College before transferring. After joining the Indian Civil Service in 1941, he opted for Pakistan after independence in 1947 and served in various provincial roles, including secretary of the irrigation department in North-West Frontier Province until 1955. In 1956, he became Home Secretary in Sindh and later Secretary of the Department of Development and Irrigation. In 1958, he was promoted to the federal level as Secretary of the Ministry of Agriculture, appointed by President Ayub Khan. He served on the Board of Governors of the Water and Power Development Authority (WAPDA) since 1958 and became its chairman in 1961, playing a key role in the construction and financial development of the Mangla Dam and Warsak Dam. From 1966 to 1970, he served as Finance Secretary. After the 1971 war, he was appointed Governor of the State Bank of Pakistan by Prime Minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto, where he questioned the socialist economic policies of Bhutto. In 1975, he became Defence Secretary, a role that brought him into close contact with the military and enabled him to manage Pakistan's atomic bomb program. He supported the nuclear initiative, backed Abdul Qadeer Khan, and helped establish the Engineering Research Laboratories (ERL) in Kahuta, heading the Uranium Coordination Board (UCB) and approving key personnel and funding. He earned the nickname "Mr Nuke" from U.S. diplomats and "Baba Atom Bomb" from the media. After Bhutto's ousting in 1977, Khan supported General Zia-ul-Haq's rise to power and was appointed Finance Minister by Zia, overseeing economic recovery and implementing policies such as risk-free interest rates and industrial corporatization, which led to Pakistan's fastest-growing economy in South Asia. He supported Zia's Islamization and the 1984 referendum. In 1985, he became Chairman of the Senate and remained in that role until 1988. After Zia's death, Khan served as acting president under constitutional succession until general elections in 1988, when he was elected president on 13 December as the consensus candidate of the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad and Pakistan People's Party, becoming the oldest person to serve as president. As president, he clashed with Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto over judicial appointments and military leadership, particularly the appointment of military chiefs. He used the Eighth Amendment to dismiss Bhutto's government in 1990 on charges of corruption and misgovernance, leading to fresh elections. In 1993, he dismissed Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on similar grounds, though the Supreme Court overturned the dismissal, resulting in a political deadlock that ultimately led to both men resigning. Khan founded the Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute of Engineering Sciences and Technology in 1988 with financial support from the BCCI, inviting A.Q. Khan as professor of physics and Asghar Qadir as professor of mathematics. He retired from public life in 1993, avoided media contact, and died from pneumonia on 27 October 2006. His legacy is viewed contentiously: he is credited with personal austerity but criticized for autocratic actions, including the dismissal of two governments. His family remains politically active; his son-in-laws include Anwar Saifullah Khan and Irfanullah Khan Marwat, and his granddaughter Samar Haroon Bilour married Haroon Bilour and Omar Ayub Khan, grandson of Ayub Khan.
